section_1.title: The Perspective Problem
section_1.content: Introduce the concept that the same physical point can be described by different sets of coordinates depending on the 'grid' (basis) we use. Define the goal: finding the mathematical 'translator' between these grids.
section_1.example: Imagine a robot named 'Z-4' standing in a room. You describe its position using the floor tiles (Standard Basis), but the robot describes positions based on its own slanted orientation (Custom Basis). The physical robot hasn't moved, but the numbers in our reports are different.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: What is a Basis?
section_2.content: Briefly refresh the concept of basis vectors. Visualize the standard basis (i-hat, j-hat) as a perfect square grid. Explain that any two non-parallel vectors can form a new coordinate system (a new grid).
section_2.example: Visual: An animation showing the standard i=(1,0), j=(0,1) grid morphing/tilting into a new grid defined by vectors b1=(2,1) and b2=(-1,1).

section_3.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (The Translator)
section_3.content: Explain how to build the 'Transition Matrix' (P). Key Concept: The columns of this matrix are simply the new basis vectors expressed in the language of the old (standard) basis.
section_3.example: If our new basis vectors are B1 = [2, 1] and B2 = [-1, 1], we line them up to create Matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]]. This matrix 'translates' coordinates from the Robot's language back to our Standard language.

section_4.title: The Coordinate Transformation Formula
section_4.content: Introduce the formula: [x]_{standard} = P * [x]_{new}. Visualize this as taking a coordinate in the skewed grid and 'scaling/rotating' it back to the square grid.
section_4.example: If the Robot says it is at position (1, 1) in its own grid, we multiply Matrix P by [1, 1]. Calculation: [2-1, 1+1] = (1, 2). Graphically show the point landing on (1, 2) on the standard XY plane.

section_5.title: Reversing the Process (The Inverse)
section_5.content: How do we go from Standard Basis to the New Basis? Introduce the inverse matrix (P⁻¹). Explain that if P takes us 'Home', P⁻¹ takes us 'Into the New World'.
section_5.example: To tell the robot to move to our point (3, 3), we don't give it (3, 3). We multiply (3, 3) by the inverse of P to find the coordinates in the robot's specific tilted grid.

section_6.title: Summary & Visual Recap
section_6.content: Summarize that 'Change of Basis' is just a change of perspective. The Transition Matrix is the bridge between these perspectives. Show a final animation of a vector staying still while the background grid swaps between standard and custom.
section_6.example: Analogy: It's like converting currency. The 'Value' (the vector) stays the same, but the 'Units' (the basis) change depending on which country (coordinate system) you are in.

section_1.title: The Perspective Problem
section_1.content: Introduce the concept that the same physical point can be described by different sets of coordinates depending on the 'grid' (basis) we use. Define the goal: finding the mathematical 'translator' between these grids.
section_1.example: Imagine a robot named 'Z-4' standing in a room. You describe its position using the floor tiles (Standard Basis), but the robot describes positions based on its own slanted orientation (Custom Basis). The physical robot hasn't moved, but the numbers in our reports are different.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: What is a Basis?
section_2.content: Briefly refresh the concept of basis vectors. Visualize the standard basis (i-hat, j-hat) as a perfect square grid. Explain that any two non-parallel vectors can form a new coordinate system (a new grid).
section_2.example: Visual: An animation showing the standard i=(1,0), j=(0,1) grid morphing/tilting into a new grid defined by vectors b1=(2,1) and b2=(-1,1).

section_3.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (The Translator)
section_3.content: Explain how to build the 'Transition Matrix' (P). Key Concept: The columns of this matrix are simply the new basis vectors expressed in the language of the old (standard) basis.
section_3.example: If our new basis vectors are B1 = [2, 1] and B2 = [-1, 1], we line them up to create Matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]]. This matrix 'translates' coordinates from the Robot's language back to our Standard language.

section_4.title: The Coordinate Transformation Formula
section_4.content: Introduce the formula: [x]_{standard} = P * [x]_{new}. Visualize this as taking a coordinate in the skewed grid and 'scaling/rotating' it back to the square grid.
section_4.example: If the Robot says it is at position (1, 1) in its own grid, we multiply Matrix P by [1, 1]. Calculation: [2-1, 1+1] = (1, 2). Graphically show the point landing on (1, 2) on the standard XY plane.

section_5.title: Reversing the Process (The Inverse)
section_5.content: How do we go from Standard Basis to the New Basis? Introduce the inverse matrix (P⁻¹). Explain that if P takes us 'Home', P⁻¹ takes us 'Into the New World'.
section_5.example: To tell the robot to move to our point (3, 3), we don't give it (3, 3). We multiply (3, 3) by the inverse of P to find the coordinates in the robot's specific tilted grid.

section_6.title: Summary & Visual Recap
section_6.content: Summarize that 'Change of Basis' is just a change of perspective. The Transition Matrix is the bridge between these perspectives. Show a final animation of a vector staying still while the background grid swaps between standard and custom.
section_6.example: Analogy: It's like converting currency. The 'Value' (the vector) stays the same, but the 'Units' (the basis) change depending on which country (coordinate system) you are in.

I have completed the code for **Section 1: The Perspective Problem**. 

The implementation features:
1.  **Strict 1:1 Synchronization**: Each of the three lecture lines corresponds to a distinct animation step.
2.  **Dual Grid System**: 
    - A standard white grid representing the "floor tiles" (Standard Basis).
    - A slanted blue grid representing the robot's "custom grid" (Basis: $b_1=(2,1), b_2=(-1,1)$).
3.  **Visual Anchor System**: All visual elements are positioned within the designated 6x6 grid on the right side of the screen using the `place_in_area` method (spanning B2 to F6).
4.  **Coordinate Highlighting**: The code visualizes how the same physical point "Z-4" at $(2, 1)_{std}$ is simultaneously represented as $(1, 0)_{blue}$ in the slanted basis.
5.  **Clean Layout**: Adheres to all margin constraints (avoiding Row A and Column 1 for primary visuals) to ensure no overlap with the title or lecture notes.

```python
from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets)
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Data from shared state
        title_text = "The Perspective Problem"
        lecture_lines = [
            "One point can have different coordinates in different grids.",
            "We describe its position using standard floor tiles.",
            "The robot uses its own tilted, custom grid."
        ]
        
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)
        
        # Colors
        COLOR_STD = WHITE
        COLOR_SLANTED = "#5271FF"
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Step 1: Show a point at (2,1) on a white square grid (#FFFFFF). Label it 'Z-4' in white (#FFFFFF).
        
        std_grid = NumberPlane(
            x_range=[-4, 4], 
            y_range=[-4, 4], 
            background_line_style={"stroke_color": COLOR_STD, "stroke_opacity": 0.3},
            axis_config={"stroke_color": COLOR_STD, "stroke_width": 1}
        )
        self.place_in_area(std_grid, "B2", "F6", scale_factor=0.5)
        
        pos_z4 = std_grid.c2p(2, 1)
        z4_dot = Dot(pos_z4, color=COLOR_STD)
        z4_label = MathTex(r"\text{Z-4}", font_size=24, color=COLOR_STD)
        z4_label.next_to(z4_dot, UL, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(
            Create(std_grid),
            FadeIn(z4_dot),
            Write(z4_label),
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(COLOR_STD),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Step 2: Fade in a slanted blue grid (#5271FF) defined by basis vectors b1=(2,1) and b2=(-1,1).
        
        slanted_grid = NumberPlane(
            x_range=[-4, 4], 
            y_range=[-4, 4], 
            background_line_style={"stroke_color": COLOR_SLANTED, "stroke_opacity": 0.6},
            axis_config={"stroke_color": COLOR_SLANTED, "stroke_width": 2}
        )
        # Apply transformation matrix mapping standard basis to basis {(2,1), (-1,1)}
        # Matrix = [[2, -1], [1, 1]]
        slanted_grid.apply_matrix([[2, -1], [1, 1]])
        self.place_in_area(slanted_grid, "B2", "F6", scale_factor=0.5)
        
        self.play(
            Create(slanted_grid),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_STD),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Step 3: Highlight coordinates (2,1) in the standard grid and (1,0) in the blue grid for the same point.
        
        # Standard projections
        h_line = std_grid.get_horizontal_line(pos_z4, color=COLOR_STD, stroke_width=1)
        v_line = std_grid.get_vertical_line(pos_z4, color=COLOR_STD, stroke_width=1)
        std_coords = MathTex("(2, 1)_{std}", color=COLOR_STD, font_size=24)
        std_coords.next_to(z4_dot, DR, buff=0.1)
        
        # Slanted highlight (vector along first basis direction)
        slanted_vec = Arrow(
            std_grid.get_origin(), 
            pos_z4, 
            buff=0, 
            color=COLOR_SLANTED, 
            stroke_width=4
        )
        slanted_coords = MathTex("(1, 0)_{blue}", color=COLOR_SLANTED, font_size=24)
        slanted_coords.next_to(z4_dot, UR, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(
            Create(h_line),
            Create(v_line),
            Write(std_coords),
            GrowArrow(slanted_vec),
            Write(slanted_coords),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(COLOR_STD),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(3)
```

    def construct(self):
        # Helper function to create a matrix using Text since LaTeX is unavailable
        def create_text_matrix(values, color=WHITE, font_size=24):
            # Create elements as Text mobjects
            matrix_elements = VGroup(*[
                VGroup(*[Text(str(cell), font_size=font_size) for cell in row]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.5)
                for row in values
            ]).arrange(DOWN, buff=0.3)
            
            # Create brackets using Text and scaling them
            bracket_l = Text("[", font_size=font_size * 2).scale(1.2)
            bracket_r = Text("]", font_size=font_size * 2).scale(1.2)

            bracket_r.sketch_to_fit_height = None # Cleanup check
            bracket_r.stretch_to_fit_height(matrix_elements.height + 0.2)

            bracket_r.next_to(matrix_elements, RIGHT, buff=0.1)
            
            res = VGroup(bracket_l, matrix_elements, bracket_r).set_color(color)
            res.elements = matrix_elements # Reference for easier manipulation
            return res

        # 1. Title and Introduction
        title = Text("The Change of Basis Matrix (The Translator)", font_size=36)
        title.to_edge(UP, buff=0.5)
        
        description = Text(
            "Converts coordinates between different coordinate systems.",

        self.play(FadeIn(description))
